analysis.one_liner: Replaces asbestos lawsuits with a no-fault federal compensation fund paid for by the companies and insurers responsible.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary chairman introduced this asbestos compensation fund with bipartisan support and held a hearing, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would shut down asbestos lawsuits in state and federal courts and move all claims into a new Office of Asbestos Disease Compensation at the Labor Department, which would pay set amounts to people with asbestos-related diseases without anyone having to prove a company was at fault. The fund would be paid for entirely by the defendant companies and insurers that faced asbestos liability, not by taxpayers. It would also create medical monitoring and mesothelioma research programs, and ban the manufacture and sale of asbestos-containing products.
analysis.who_benefits: People with asbestos-related diseases, including terminal mesothelioma patients, would get guaranteed, faster, no-fault compensation without years of litigation, plus legal help and medical monitoring programs. Companies with asbestos liability and their insurers would also benefit: they would pay mandatory but capped, predictable assessments into the fund instead of facing open-ended jury verdicts, and the litigation that pushed many firms into bankruptcy would end.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Asbestos victims and the companies liable to them

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a no-fault, nonadversarial compensation office in the Labor Department so claimants do not have to prove negligence or fight companies in court [S2][S3].
Prioritizes and expedites payment for terminal health claims, including mesothelioma patients with less than a year to live, with initial payments due within 30 days of an accepted settlement [S3].
Funds the program privately through mandatory assessments on defendant companies and their insurers, with the bill stating it is not intended to increase the federal deficit or burden taxpayers [S3].

Creates medical monitoring programs for exposed people, a national mesothelioma research and treatment program, and bans the manufacture, processing, or distribution of asbestos-containing products within three years [S2].
Caps attorneys' fees at 5% of an award so more of the compensation goes to claimants, and provides claimant assistance and pro bono legal rosters [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Asbestos defendant companies and their insurers, which would pay mandatory assessments into the fund based on their past asbestos liability. Claimants would also give up something: their right to a jury trial and potentially larger court awards, accepting fixed award amounts instead.
analysis.who_pays_short: Asbestos companies, insurers, and claimants' court rights

drawbacks.text: Awards would be fixed by a statutory schedule and reduced by any prior compensation, rather than set by a jury, and a pending lawsuit would be stayed the moment the act passed — so many claimants would likely receive less than they might win in court [S2][S3].

Claims must meet strict medical criteria to be eligible, and the bill expressly provides no federal bailout if the fund runs short of money — the risk of an underfunded fund falls on sick claimants [S3].

The bill would end most court claims even for people already mid-lawsuit, and attorney fee caps and nonadversarial processing could make it harder for claimants to get experienced representation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For terminal patients, guaranteed faster payment without litigation is a real gain, and ending asbestos manufacturing is a clear public health win. But the trade-off is genuine: sick people would exchange the right to have a jury value their injury for fixed awards that critics on the victims' side argued were too low, under strict medical criteria, from a fund with no taxpayer backstop if it ran out of money. Whether the trade favors claimants depends almost entirely on whether the fund is adequately financed over decades.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, placed on the Senate calendar, and the Judiciary Committee held a hearing on it, but no committee vote or floor vote ever happened before that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Arlen Specter introduced the Fairness in Asbestos Injury Resolution Act of 2006 on May 26, 2006, joined by Sen. Patrick Leahy [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on June 5, 2006 [S5].
The Senate Judiciary Committee held hearings on the bill on June 7, 2006 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee markup or a Senate floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Asbestos defendant companies and insurers avoided the mandatory funding obligations, while asbestos victims kept access to the courts but got no new guaranteed compensation system.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Asbestos companies and insurers; victims kept courts only

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, delivered introductory remarks, and got it placed on the Senate calendar; his committee held hearings on it.

for.name: 5 cosponsors (4 Republicans, 1 Democrat)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill support from both parties.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote despite its placement on the calendar.

against.name: Asbestos plaintiffs' trial lawyers
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill, arguing the fixed awards and strict medical criteria would leave many victims with less than they would win in court.

against.name: Labor and victim advocates skeptical of fund size
against.what_they_did: Raised concerns that the fund's financing was inadequate and that sick workers would bear the risk if it ran short.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican chairman and a Democratic ranking member, with 4 Republican and 1 Democratic cosponsors — and opposition came from both parties' flanks rather than a party-line split.

industries.industry: Asbestos defendant companies (building materials, auto parts, shipbuilding, and other former asbestos users)
industries.note: The bill would have replaced open-ended jury verdicts and bankruptcies with capped, predictable mandatory payments into a fund that compensates the sick. Their gain in certainty came at the cost of decades of assessments.

Insurers would pay fixed assessments set by an Asbestos Insurers Commission in which they participated, in exchange for ending uncertain litigation exposure. Their certainty gain ran alongside the fund paying victims.
Attorneys' fees would be capped at 5% of awards and the adversarial litigation system their practices depend on would close, redirecting most compensation money to claimants themselves.

industries.industry: Manufacturers, importers, and distributors of asbestos-containing products
industries.note: The bill bans manufacture, processing, and distribution of asbestos-containing products within three years, eliminating those product lines.
